plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a vertical bar chart of twelve blue bars on a pale blue field, showing strain energy as a function of cycloalkane ring size. The horizontal axis is labeled Ring size and ticked at every integer from 3 to 14. The same quantity is given two vertical scales: the left axis, labeled Strain energy (kJ/mol), runs from 0 to 120 in steps of 20 with horizontal gridlines, and the right axis, labeled (kcal/mol), runs from 0 to 28.7 with tick labels 4.8, 9.6, 14.3, 19.1 and 23.9. Bars stand at every ring size except 6 and 14; at those two positions a short downward arrow with the numeral 0 above it points to the baseline in place of a bar. The two tallest bars sit at the left, about 115 kJ/mol at ring size 3 and slightly above 110 at ring size 4. The height then falls abruptly to roughly 26 at 5 and 25 at 7, rises through 40 at 8 to a secondary maximum near 53 at 9, eases to 50 at 10 and 46 at 11, drops to about 10 at 12, and returns to 22 at 13. The profile is jagged rather than smooth, so the eye tracks an irregular march of strain across ring sizes rather than a trend. The chart presents the strain energies obtained by subtracting an acyclic reference heat of combustion per CH2 unit and scaling by the number of CH2 units in the ring.

interactionPlan.concept: Cycloalkane strain energy varies irregularly with ring size, dropping to zero for cyclohexane (6) before rising again for medium-sized rings due to transannular interactions.
elements: x-axis labeled 'Ring size' with integer ticks from 3 to 14
left y-axis labeled 'Strain energy (kJ/mol)' with ticks from 0 to 120 in steps of 20
right y-axis labeled '(kcal/mol)' with ticks corresponding to the left axis (4.8, 9.6, 14.3, 19.1, 23.9, 28.7)
horizontal gridlines aligned with the y-axis ticks over a light blue background field
solid blue data bars at ring sizes 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13
downward-pointing arrows with the numeral '0' at the baseline for ring sizes 6 and 14

interactions.teaches: Sweeping through ring sizes reveals the non-monotonic nature of strain energy, highlighting exact values and the irregular peaks at small (3-4) and medium (8-11) rings.
interactions.label: Ring size

interactions.teaches: Cyclohexane (6) and very large rings (like 14) are strain-free in this comparison, acting as the stable reference points.

demo_steps.title: Small rings have high strain
demo_steps.narration: Small rings like cyclopropane (3) and cyclobutane (4) possess very high strain energy due to severe angle compression.

demo_steps.title: Zero strain in cyclohexane
demo_steps.narration: At a ring size of 6, strain drops completely to zero because cyclohexane can adopt a perfectly staggered chair conformation with ideal bond angles.

demo_steps.title: Transannular strain in medium rings
demo_steps.narration: Strain energy rises again for medium-sized rings (8-11), peaking around 9. This is due to transannular strain—steric clashes between hydrogen atoms across the interior of the ring.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Strain energy does not simply decrease as rings get larger; it drops to zero at cyclohexane (6), rises again for medium rings due to internal crowding, and eventually vanishes for large rings.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Standard 2D bar chart with a light blue background fill behind the plotting area. Left (kJ/mol) and right (kcal/mol) y-axes must perfectly align their ticks and horizontal gridlines. Use tall, solid blue bars for sizes 3 and 4 (~115 and ~110 kJ/mol). Leave clear gaps at 6 and 14, occupied only by small downward arrows and '0' labels pointing precisely at the x-axis baseline. The secondary peak around 9-10 should be visibly roughly half the height of the first peak.

authoredContext:
Because the heat of combustion of a cycloalkane depends on size, we need to look at heats of combustion per CH2 unit. Subtracting a reference value derived from a strain-free acyclic alkane and then multiplying by the number of CH2 units in the ring gives the overall strain energy. The figure shows the results.

The data in the figure show that Baeyer’s theory is only partially correct. Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are indeed strained, just as predicted, but cyclopentane is more strained than predicted, and cyclohexane is strain-free. Cycloalkanes of intermediate size have only modest strain, and rings of 14 carbons or more are strain-free. Why is Baeyer’s theory wrong?

Cycloalkane strain energies, as calculated by taking the difference between cycloalkane heat of combustion per CH2 and acyclic alkane heat of combustion per CH2, and multiplying by the number of CH2 units in a ring. Small and medium rings are strained, but cyclohexane rings and very large rings are strain-free.

Bar graph shows strain energies in cycloalkanes with strain energy in kilojoules per mole and kilocalories per mol for various ring sizes from 3-14. Strain energy is highest for 3-carbon ring.

discrepancies: The x-axis tick marks are centered on the labels and bars, whereas the source figure places the tick marks between the categories as separators.
The right y-axis title '(kcal/mol)' is rotated to read top-to-bottom (standard for right-side axes in the library), whereas the source figure rotates it bottom-to-top to match the left axis.
evaluation.notes: Excellent reproduction of the source figure with exact data values, correct dual axes, perfect custom annotations for zero-strain rings, and a highly effective interactive demo player that walks through the key concepts.
action_items: To match the source's x-axis tick placement exactly, configure the x-axis grid with `drawTicks: true` and `offset: true` but move the ticks to the boundaries, or use custom drawing for the separator ticks.
The right y-axis title can be forced to read bottom-to-top by drawing it manually using a plugin instead of relying on the default Chart.js scale title, though this is a very minor aesthetic detail.
